name: Teriparatide
evidenceNote: Approved in 2002 on a randomized, placebo-controlled fracture trial in 1,637 postmenopausal women, with further controlled trials in men and in glucocorticoid-induced osteoporosis.
summary: Teriparatide is the active front section of parathyroid hormone, given as a daily injection. It is FDA-approved to build bone in high-risk osteoporosis.
keyTakeaway: Teriparatide is a recombinant fragment of parathyroid hormone: the opening 34-amino-acid stretch that carries nearly all of the hormone's activity. Injected once a day, it stimulates bone-building cells more than bone-removing ones, so it adds new bone rather than only slowing loss. Approved by the FDA in 2002 as Forteo, it cut new spine fractures from 14.3% to 5.0% in its pivotal trial. Generic versions are now approved too. Rats given high doses developed bone cancer, so use beyond two years is reserved for people still at high fracture risk.

blocks.text: Parathyroid hormone (PTH) is an 84-amino-acid hormone made by four small glands in the neck, and it is the body's main regulator of calcium and phosphate in bone and kidney [1]. Teriparatide reproduces only its first 34 amino acids, the section that does the biological work. It binds PTH receptors as strongly as the full hormone and has the same effects on bone and kidney [1].

The version sold by Eli Lilly as Forteo is made by recombinant DNA technology in E. coli bacteria [1]. It belongs to a small group of anabolic, or bone-building, osteoporosis drugs, in contrast to the more common antiresorptive drugs such as bisphosphonates, which work by slowing bone breakdown.

Bone is constantly remodelled: osteoclasts remove old bone and osteoblasts lay down new bone. A single daily dose of teriparatide stimulates osteoblasts more than osteoclasts, so new bone forms on both the spongy inner bone and the dense outer layer [1]. In people this shows up as more skeletal mass, higher markers of bone turnover, and stronger bone [1].

Timing is the key. The same hormone at a constant high level, as in hyperparathyroidism (an overactive parathyroid gland), harms the skeleton because breakdown then outpaces building [1]. Daily injections create a short pulse instead. Calcium in the blood rises for a few hours, peaking about four to six hours after a dose, and is back to baseline by 16 hours [1].

Yes. Forteo was approved on November 26, 2002, and is still marketed by Lilly [3]. The label lists the first US approval of teriparatide as 1987, which predates Forteo; that earlier injectable, Parathar, is now listed as discontinued [1][6]. Several other teriparatide products have since been approved, including Bonsity in 2019 and generic versions from 2023 onward [4][5].

items.text: The pivotal fracture trial in 1,637 postmenopausal women is published [2].
FDA approves Bonsity, another teriparatide injection [4].
The first generic teriparatide injections are approved, including one from Apotex [5].

blocks.text: The label covers three groups at high risk of fracture, or who have failed or cannot tolerate other osteoporosis treatment: postmenopausal women with osteoporosis; men with primary or hypogonadal (low testosterone) osteoporosis; and men and women with osteoporosis caused by long-term glucocorticoid (steroid) use at 5 mg a day of prednisone or more [1].

The pivotal trial randomized 1,637 postmenopausal women who already had spine fractures to daily injections of 20 or 40 mcg or placebo, all with calcium and vitamin D, for a median of 21 months of observation [2]. On 20 mcg, new spine fractures fell from 14% to 5% and new non-spine fragility fractures from 6% to 3%, and spine bone density rose 9 percentage points more than on placebo [2].

rows: Rose in 94% of men over a median 10 months [1]

blocks.text: In men and in glucocorticoid users, the trials measured bone density rather than fractures, which is why the men's indication is worded as increasing bone mass [1]. The label adds that use for more than two years in a lifetime should only be considered for people who remain, or again become, at high risk of fracture [1].

In the main trials, the most common side effects were joint pain, general pain and nausea; joint pain affected 10.1% on teriparatide against 8.4% on placebo, and leg cramps 2.6% against 1.3% [1]. At least one short-lived episode of raised blood calcium a few hours after a dose occurred in 11% of women and 6% of men on the drug [1]. A brief drop in blood pressure on standing, which can cause lightheadedness, was seen in 5% of volunteers in short-term studies, mostly with the first doses [1].

The main concern comes from rats. In two-year rat studies, osteosarcoma, a malignant bone tumor, appeared at every dose tested and reached 40% to 50% of animals in the highest-dose groups [1]. In people, rare cases have been reported after approval, but two large US insurance claims studies found 3 cases among 379,283 users and none among 153,316, a rate similar to comparison groups [1]. The label still advises avoiding it in people at higher baseline risk: children and young adults with growing bones, Paget's disease of bone, prior skeletal cancer or bone metastases, and past radiation therapy involving the skeleton [1].
